_comment: packaging/release-exclude.json — WHAT MAY NOT LEAVE THIS MACHINE, in ONE place.
Read by scripts/release-tree.mjs, which is called by BOTH release builders:
scripts/build-public-tree.sh   the fresh public repository
scripts/build-zip.sh           the clean and portable zips (never `mine`)
WHY ONE FILE AND NOT TWO LISTS. Until now build-public-tree.sh held the list and
build-zip.sh held none, and the two artefacts drifted exactly as far apart as that
sounds: the public tree removed the private test suite, the portable zip shipped
`git archive HEAD` — i.e. everything tracked — and printed 'verified: no personal
content' while carrying a colleague's email address, two internal IPv4s, a NAS share
path and 33 of the author's real memories in a fixture directory named after him.
Both builders now read THIS file, so an exclusion added for one artefact cannot be
missing from the other. Adding a path here is the whole edit.
THIS IS THE PROMISE, NOT THE PROOF. scripts/check-release-clean.mjs is the proof, and
both builders run it against the STAGED tree and refuse to produce an artefact if it
finds anything. A list of exclusions maintained by hand has been re-read and found
wrong twice; the gate is what catches the miss.
`keep` IS DELIBERATELY POSITIVE. `test` is excluded wholesale and the two shippable
subtrees are named back in, so a NEW file under test/ is private BY DEFAULT and only
these paths can ever ship. Naming 60 exclusions instead would make the next new
fixture public by accident.

exclude.why: THE PRIVATE SUITE. 9,400 lines asserting against one particular corpus — it fails for anyone else — and it holds internal host addresses, a colleague's real email, the author's own address, a NAS share path, and test/fixtures/projects/ which is a copy of his memory folder (33 .md files). Excluding it removes an entire class of exposure and costs the recipient nothing they could have used. A synthetic fixture corpus would let it ship one day; that is a separate project. See `keep` for the two subtrees that DO ship.
This workflow greps for a live credential BY VALUE, to prove it is absent from a built zip — so the file CONTAINS the credential.

Same: it names the credential in order to assert its absence. NOTE both are excluded BY NAME, never by directory — excluding all of .github/workflows/ also dropped ci.yml and left the published repo with NO CI, the first thing a reviewer looks for. ci.yml names no credential and is scanned by the gate like everything else that ships.

It drives test/recall-stress/, which does not ship — a workflow that references a path excluded from the tree is exactly the failure class scripts/audit-read-paths.mjs exists for, in a file format that checker cannot read. The SCRIPT half of the job does ship (test/public/campaign-lite.mjs); only the author's scheduling of it does not.

The author's own packaging: it embeds their paths and their memory folder, and a recipient of a zip has nothing to build. (It is also the script that reads this file — a build tool need not ship in its own output.)
Benchmark fixture written from real customer questions; names customers and product models.
Measurement harness bound to the author's corpus.
Measurement harness bound to the author's corpus; reads test/currency-questions.json, which does not ship.
Measurement harness bound to the author's corpus.
Measurement harness; carries a NAS share path and an internal hostname.

READS A FIXTURE THAT DOES NOT SHIP (scripts/probes.json or test/*.json), so in a release tree it is guaranteed to throw. Found by auditing the staged tree for live references to excluded paths rather than by assuming the first exclusion list was right — scripts/audit-read-paths.mjs now does that automatically, in both builders.
Same class: unguarded read of a fixture that does not ship.
Same class: unguarded read of a fixture that does not ship.
Same class: unguarded read of a fixture that does not ship.
Holds benchmark questions written from the author's corpus, naming a real competitor. Found by a vendor-term sweep of the STAGED tree rather than of the repo.
Same as measure-graph-spread.js: benchmark questions written from the author's corpus, naming a real competitor.

Unguarded top-level readFileSync of a test/ fixture, so it throws ENOENT on a public clone. This was the one that mattered: it is an npm script, so `npm run eval:state` died for anyone who tried it. Found by RUNNING every npm script on a fresh install, not by re-reading this list.
Same class as eval-state.
Same class as eval-state.
Same class as eval-state.

Question set written against the author's corpus, naming an internal tool. Caught by the gate rather than by reading this list. scripts/measure-index-memory.js is deliberately NOT here — it takes an index path and asserts nothing about content.

UNPROVEN INSTRUMENTATION DOES NOT SHIP. The ordinary-word probe is a measurement running against the author's corpus under a pre-registration, and its own reading rule says it earns a PROPOSAL, not a behaviour. lib/search.js imports it lazily and optionally for exactly this reason, and searching is unaffected by its absence (asserted in the suite).

keep.why: A suite that runs only on fixtures — no author corpus, no clock, no dependence on how many documents exist. It is what `npm test` is repointed at in a release tree, and it is the suite the Windows hand-off runs.
16 committed memories about a bike workshop — a frozen synthetic corpus the public suite asserts against.

🟥 MEM-68/U-2. 92 lines of env-var names and a join() — no corpus, no addresses, nothing personal — and the ONE consumer that ships, test/public/campaign-lite.mjs, deliberately inlines the same list and cross-checks itself against this file as TEXT. Excluding it had two costs, both found on a real upgrade (campaign D.4): unzipping over an older install leaves the OLD copy on disk, so the cross-check compares today's inlined list against a stale one and a harness author who reads the list from the install gets whichever version that install happens to hold (1.7.0's had 15 entries, 1.7.1's 20); and in a fresh install the cross-check has nothing to read and is silently vacuous. Shipping it makes the upgrade overwrite the stale copy and gives the assertion something true to compare against in every artefact.
